title: The kiswah
hookLine: the black cloth with gold verses is renewed each year at Hajj
carry: a new cloth for the house

cards: In a workshop, a craftsman bends over a stretched length of black silk. His needle carries gold-colored thread. Stitch by stitch, a letter rises off the cloth, raised and shining, part of a line of the Qur'an.
Beside him another worker is on a different letter of the same word. Nobody here is making a garment for a person.
They are dressing a building, a plain cube of stone in Mecca that people around the world turn toward every day. The black in photographs of the Ka'ba is not its wall. It's a garment.

teach.h: KISWAH: A GARMENT FOR THE HOUSE.
teach.b: First, the word. Kiswah is the Arabic word for clothing, a garment. The Ka'ba's walls are stone; the kiswah is what it wears.

teach.h: A RESORT FOR MANKIND AND A SANCTUARY.
teach.b: The Qur'an remembers Abraham and the House, and says, in Pickthall's words, that God made the House "a resort for mankind and a sanctuary." A place people return to.
The kiswah honors that House the way a family might set out its best cloth for a guest. Third, an old custom.
A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari, from Aisha, the Prophet's wife, says that before the fast of Ramadan was made a duty, people fasted on a certain day, and that was the day the Ka'ba was covered.

So the covering is older than the Ramadan fast. For a long stretch of later history, the new cloth was made in Egypt and traveled to Mecca with the Cairo caravan we followed yesterday, greeted in the streets as it left.
Today it's made in Mecca itself, in a workshop set up for that one task. Fourth, the renewal.
Once a year a new kiswah is hung and the old one comes down.

teach.h: A NEW CLOTH FOR THE HOUSE.
teach.b: Tradition says the old cloth is cut into pieces and given away, and some pieces end up framed in homes and museums far from Mecca.
Near the top runs a gold band of Qur'an verses worked in thread, and lower down, panels of calligraphy around the door. A cube of stone, given a new garment every year.

how: Once a year a new kiswah, made in Mecca from black silk with Qur'anic verses in gold and silver thread, is hung on the Ka'ba, and pieces of the old cloth are given as gifts.

practice: Find a close photo of the kiswah's gold band or door curtain, or picture it: black cloth, a band of gold letters running around the cube.
Don't try to read every word; follow one stroke with your eyes from where it starts to where it curls and ends, then another, knowing somebody stitched each curve by hand.
If you pray, let one verse you know rise in your mind; if not, simply admire the patience.
